key_terms.meaning: R opposes current; v = iR, and p = vi = i²R is dissipated as heat.
L links flux to current; v = L di/dt, and energy = ½Li² is stored in the magnetic field.
C links charge to voltage; i = C dv/dt, and energy = ½Cv² is stored in the electric field.
A source whose voltage or current is fixed by its own value, not by another circuit variable.
A source whose value is a constant multiple of a voltage or current elsewhere, such as k v_x or g i_x.
For a resistor, v = iR at constant temperature; R is the resistance in ohms.
The algebraic sum of currents leaving a node is zero: Σ i = 0.
The algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero: Σ v = 0.
A point where two or more circuit elements meet; a node has one voltage with respect to a chosen reference.
A single element or a series path between two nodes, carrying one current.
Any closed path through the circuit that starts and ends at the same node.
A loop that contains no other loop inside it; used in mesh analysis.
A connected set of branches that touches every node and has no closed path.
Elements joined end to end so the same current passes through each.
Elements joined across the same two nodes so each has the same voltage.
For series resistors, v_k = v_total R_k / R_eq.
Replaces a voltage source V_s in series with R_s by a current source I_s = V_s/R_s in parallel with R_s, and the reverse.
Converts a three-terminal star of resistors into an equivalent delta, or a delta into a star, preserving terminal currents and voltages.
One chord plus the tree path that closes it; it gives an independent KVL equation.
A minimal set of branches whose removal splits the graph; it gives an independent KCL equation.

takeaways: Every passive element is defined by its V-I relation, not by its shape or name.
Resistors dissipate energy, inductors store it in a magnetic field, and capacitors store it in an electric field.
An independent source fixes its own value; a dependent source is controlled by another voltage or current.
KCL follows charge conservation at a node; KVL follows energy conservation around a closed path.
Counting nodes, branches and loops tells how many independent equations a circuit needs.
Series and parallel reduction plus divider rules solve many circuits without full analysis.
Star-delta and source transformations change the diagram, not the terminal behaviour.
A tree gives a systematic way to choose independent tie-set and cut-set equations.
bank_note: The syllabi stress clear sign convention, independent-equation counting, and step-by-step reduction before applying network theorems.

bank.q: Define resistance, inductance and capacitance. Write the V-I relation and energy expression for each, and state whether the element dissipates or stores energy.
outline: Write v = iR and p = i²R for resistance; energy is dissipated.
Write v = L di/dt and energy = ½Li² for inductance; energy is stored in the magnetic field.
Write i = C dv/dt and energy = ½Cv² for capacitance; energy is stored in the electric field.
State the passive sign convention used for each relation.

bank.q: Distinguish an independent voltage source from a dependent voltage source. Give one example of each type of dependent source and explain what sets its value.
outline: Independent source value is fixed by the source itself.
Dependent source value is k times a voltage or current elsewhere.
Examples include VCVS, CCVS, VCCS and CCCS.
Explain that a dependent source acts as a controlled gain element.

bank.q: State Ohm's law, KCL and KVL. Explain the sign convention used when writing KCL at a node and KVL around a loop.
outline: Ohm's law: v = iR for a resistor.
KCL: algebraic sum of currents at a node is zero.
KVL: algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero.
Choose current directions and voltage polarities before writing equations.

bank.q: Define node, branch, loop, mesh, tree, chord and cut-set in a circuit graph. State how many tree branches and chords a connected graph with n nodes and b branches has.
outline: Define each term in one clear line.
A tree has n−1 branches.
A connected graph has b−n+1 chords.
A cut-set splits the graph into two parts; a tie-set uses one chord.

bank.q: A 12 V source drives three resistors in series: 4 Ω, 6 Ω and 10 Ω. Find the current, the voltage across each resistor and the total power dissipated.
outline: P = 12 × 0.6 = 7.2 W, or sum i²R.

bank.q: Two resistors 6 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel across a 9 V source. Use current division to find each branch current, then verify with KCL.
outline: Total current = 9/2 = 4.5 A.
KCL check: 1.5 + 3 = 4.5 A.

bank.q: Convert a 20 V source in series with 5 Ω into a current source. Then use source transformation to find the current through a 10 Ω load connected across the terminals.
outline: Place 4 A source in parallel with 5 Ω.
The 5 Ω and 10 Ω load are in parallel.
Load current = 4 × 5/(5+10) = 1.33 A.

bank.q: A delta network has resistors R_AB = 10 Ω, R_BC = 20 Ω and R_CA = 30 Ω. Find the equivalent star resistors and state the formulas used.
outline: Use R_A = R_AB R_CA/(R_AB+R_BC+R_CA).
Use R_B = R_AB R_BC/(R_AB+R_BC+R_CA).
Use R_C = R_BC R_CA/(R_AB+R_BC+R_CA).

bank.q: For the graph of a given circuit with 5 nodes and 7 branches, choose a tree and list one tie-set and one cut-set. Write the corresponding KVL and KCL equations.
outline: A tree has 5−1 = 4 branches.
The number of chords is 7−4 = 3.
One tie-set contains one chord and tree branches; write KVL around it.
One cut-set contains tree branches and chords; write KCL for it.

bank.q: Analyze a circuit with one dependent source using KCL and KVL. Explain why the dependent source cannot be treated as an independent source when writing equations, and solve for the controlling variable.
outline: Write KCL and KVL with the dependent source value as k v_x or g i_x.
Keep the controlling variable as an unknown.
Do not assign the dependent source a fixed value.
Solve the simultaneous equations and check the source value.

bank.q: Compare series and parallel reduction, voltage division and current division. For a given three-resistor network, decide which method gives the shortest solution and justify your choice.
outline: Series reduction adds resistances; parallel reduction uses reciprocal sums.
Voltage division applies to series branches; current division applies to parallel branches.
Choose by identifying a common current or a common voltage.
Justify why the chosen method needs fewer equations.

bank.q: Evaluate the statement: 'A star-delta transformation changes the power dissipated in the network.' Use terminal equivalence to justify your answer.
outline: Star-delta transformation preserves terminal voltages and currents.
Total power entering the terminals is therefore unchanged.
Power in individual resistors may change because the element set changes.
Conclude that total network power is unchanged, but element powers can differ.

bank.q: A practical voltage source is modelled as V_s in series with R_s; a practical current source as I_s in parallel with R_s. Derive the condition V_s = I_s R_s for equal terminal behaviour and discuss one limitation of the model.
outline: For the voltage source: V = V_s − I R_s.
For the current source: V = (I_s − I)R_s = I_s R_s − I R_s.
Equate the two expressions to get V_s = I_s R_s.
An ideal source with R_s = 0 or R_s = ∞ cannot be transformed.

bank.q: Using graph theory, explain how a tree selects independent KVL and KCL equations. Show that tie-sets and cut-sets give the same number of independent equations as mesh and nodal analysis.
outline: A tree has n−1 branches and b−n+1 chords.
Each chord defines a tie-set and one independent KVL equation.
Each tree branch defines a fundamental cut-set and one independent KCL equation.
Mesh analysis uses b−n+1 mesh currents in planar graphs.
Nodal analysis uses n−1 node voltages; both sets span the same solution space.

glossary.def: A single element or a series path between two nodes, carrying one current.
A branch of the graph that is not in the chosen tree; each chord closes one tie-set.
A minimal set of branches whose removal separates the graph into two parts.
A source whose voltage or current is controlled by another circuit voltage or current.
Three resistors connected in a closed triangle between three terminals.
A source that maintains a specified voltage or current regardless of other circuit variables.
A point where three or more branches meet; often used for a node with more than two connections.
The algebraic sum of currents entering a node is zero.
The algebraic sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero.
Any closed path in a circuit that starts and ends at the same node.
A loop that encloses no other loop; used in planar mesh analysis.
A point where two or more circuit elements meet.
For a resistor, voltage equals current times resistance at constant temperature.
A path with zero current because the resistance between its terminals is infinite.
Elements connected across the same two nodes, so they share the same voltage.
A circuit graph that can be drawn on a plane without branches crossing.
Elements connected end to end so the same current flows through each.
A path with zero voltage because its resistance is zero.
Replacing a voltage source in series with a resistor by an equivalent current source in parallel with the same resistor, or the reverse.
Three resistors joined at one common node and brought out to three terminals.
A conversion between a three-terminal star and an equivalent three-terminal delta.
One chord plus the tree path that closes it; it gives an independent KVL equation.
A connected set of branches that touches every node and contains no closed path.
The rule that in a series string each resistor takes a voltage proportional to its resistance.
The rule that in parallel branches each branch current is proportional to the conductance of that branch.
